attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter post, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: 'Won't do much' is firm. Treating the expected Plus increase and similar Team/Enterprise increases as the antecedent is a fair reading of 'even a $2 price increase'. Scope and wording are preserved.

contract.note: The plain reading (the increases would leave most of the losses intact) is ordinary and fair. Requiring the effect of the price changes to be isolated from other changes is reasonable. There is no deadline, so the horizon is open.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own page, available before the cutoff, still lists Plus at $20/month. This bears on the antecedent (the increase does not appear to have happened), not on the loss outcome, so it cannot contradict the claim.

reviews.rationale: This is a conditional forecast whose antecedent is the price increases. The only evidence suggests Plus is still $20, and no dated record shows the increases happened. With the antecedent unmet or unknown, the claim is not scored. No evidence isolates any price effect on losses.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter post.

semantics.note: This is essentially conditional arithmetic: at the 2024 ratio of $2.35 spent per $1 of revenue, $11.6B of revenue costs about $27.3B. The ratio antecedent and the end-of-2025 target are preserved. It is close to hypothetical arithmetic rather than a firm prediction that the ratio would persist.

contract.note: Reading 'cost of revenue' as the broad spending ratio from the context is fair. The result depends on whether the 2025 expense basis is comparable to the 2024 basis (total spend vs. figures with non-cash items stripped out), which the speaker did not define.

evidence.note: Contemporaneous 2024 projections that produce the 2.35 ratio and the $27.3B derived figure. They are baseline only, not 2025 outcomes.

The FT reports about $13B of 2025 revenue and $34B of spending, with an $8B loss once non-cash items are excluded. The expense basis is not reconciled to the 2024 figures, so whether the ratio persisted (the antecedent) is not established.

reviews.rationale: The deadline has passed and revenue exceeded the target. But whether the 2024 cost ratio persisted depends on the expense basis: about 2.6x on the $34B spending figure, much lower on the non-cash-adjusted figure. With no reconciliation in the packet, the antecedent is not established and the conditional cannot be scored.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter post.

semantics.note: A firm present-tense claim about generative AI in general, faithfully normalised.

contract.note: Reading 'generative AI' as providers generally, and 'deeply unprofitable' as substantial operating losses relative to revenue, is an ordinary reading. 'To run' could instead mean inference costs only, as his next sentence about per-call losses hints, so the interpretation matters and is flagged.

evidence.note: A forecast of OpenAI's full-year 2024 loss: one company, a projection, and not realised quarterly results for the sector.
A modelled, explicitly unverified estimate of positive API gross margins for OpenAI. It covers serving costs only, not operating profit, for one company.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no representative, comparable results for generative AI providers in Q3 2024. One company's loss forecast and one modelled gross-margin estimate point in different directions on different measures, so the evidence does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter post.

semantics.note: 'Suggests' marks an inference, but 'really has no room', 'commoditized' and the following firm lines ('It can't... OpenAI is trapped') show a firm commitment. Linking the two sentences with 'as' is a slight tightening but acceptable.

contract.note: Reading the claim as pricing power at publication, measured in the last full quarter, is fair. The result depends on whether premium-priced new models count as 'charging more', which the speaker did not settle.

evidence.note: OpenAI confirms the 99% per-token cost drop across model generations. It does not measure whether customers would accept higher prices.
o1-preview was priced well above o1-mini, which shows price tiering. A posted premium does not show sustained demand at that price.
Independent researchers found a cost and capability trade-off between the o1 models. It is not evidence of how the market responded to prices.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows differentiated, premium-priced reasoning models in Q3 2024, which cuts against 'few points of differentiation'. But there is no evidence on demand, retention or price elasticity to show whether OpenAI could sustain higher API charges, so the evidence does not settle the claim.
